Blasphemous is a dark and rather gruesome 2D metroidvania/soulslike pixel art platformer action game (do we have a better name for that genre yet?), and its uncompromising aesthetic is both seductive but, for people of a certain disposition, also rough on the senses. Let's talk for a while about its aesthetics and approach to visual representation of spiritual suffering.

Galaxy Slayer Zed is a great skin, slick, well-animated, lots of cool effects and cool visual ideas... and he doesn't fit into the Odyssey universe as we know it almost at all. His lore is kind of weak, his interactions with other characters are necessarily one-sided, and his one-note personality makes him uninteresting as a monologuing villain.

This all speaks somewhat to the difficulty of following up on such a rock-solid established universe as Odyssey, and the trouble with trying to do story-telling through sheer expansion of the character roster without also deepening the story.

From dealing with a bag of bones to dealing with a dog. There's some kind of demented symmetry there, but I can't see it because my eyes are too busy crying about the poor doggo.

Sif is an interesting boss in a few ways - it is, for one thing, not the least bit monstrous outside outside of its size. snippet.description:

--------

So, we're doing the "should [insert FromSoft game here] have an easy mode???" discussion again, are we? Well, it's that time of year, I guess. I don't often wade in on this one, but I wanted to talk about a major misconception that seems to be underpinning a lot of the discussion right now: the idea that "accessibility" = "easy mode", which is wrong for a number of reasons.

So let's talk about that.

---
USEFUL RESOURCES: 

AbleGamers - a charity focusing on making gaming accessible for the disabled. They have a number of interesting articles and resources on the subject, and are a good place to start: https://ablegamers.org/

COO of AbleGamers Steve Spohn: https://twitter.com/stevenspohn
His twitch stream: https://www.twitch.tv/steveinspawn

Disabled gamer, Halfcoordinated, on Celeste's Assist Mode: https://twitter.com/halfcoordinated/status/1113910732045864973
(His excellent twitch stream, where among other things he's playing Sekiro one-handed: https://www.twitch.tv/halfcoordinated )

Gaming accessibility expert Ian Hamilton: https://twitter.com/ianhamilton_

The Xbox Adaptive Controller as an example of what accessibility can look like: https://www.xbox.com/en-GB/xbox-one/accessories/controllers/xbox-adaptive-controller

New York Times - Adaptive Video Game Controllers Open Worlds for Gamers With Disabilities: https://www.nytimes.com/2019/02/20/business/video-game-controllers-disabilities.html

God of War is absolutely one of the best games of 2018, and we played through it over the course of nine 3-hour streams late last year and early this year.

During the playthrough I spent some time talking about the real mythology underpinning the game, and some of its narrative and aesthetic decisions about how to represent it. 2018 is dead, long live 2019. It is a time for reflection. It is a time for taking stock. It is a time for making lists of things.

Twitter: http://twitter.com/tbskyen
-----

It's famous, it's infamous, it's a story older players tell the noobs to make them scared at night. It's rancid, rickety Blighttown.

With its vine-like climbing constructions and maddening geography, it has more character than any of the other environments we've been through so far - unfortunately that character is a stark, raving lunatic with poison darts and a bug collection. Blighttown is designed to look like a place of madness, and to take the player with it into that mindset. It is a shaky grasp on reality, built on a poison bog. It is a scathing satire of the towns, castles and churches that are built on its foundations.

Blighttown is not just a level, or an environment, it is, in a very real way, a boss character in Dark Souls. So let's talk about that!

#DarkSouls #Soulsborne #BossDesignsOfDarkSouls

Anyway! The Eye in the Abyss is probably my favourite piece of League of Legends writing so far - it addresses a lot of the criticisms I've had for League's lore writing so far and does a fantastic job of using characters to ground some of the more abstract ideas of cosmic horror and the threat of the Void and the religious zeal of the Frostguard tribe in a way that makes them approachable to a reader. snippet.title: What's the deal with Hanzo & Genji? || Character design & lore discussion
snippet.description:
Join the channel discord: https://discord.gg/SWZ8zYv (25 uses only)
---
SOMETHING I FORGOT TO BRING UP IN THE VIDEO:
Hanzo is named (presumably) for Hattori Hanzo, a famous samurai in the service of Oda Nobunaga. Genji is named for Hikaru Genji, the main character in The Tale of Genji by Lady Murasaki, a story generally considered to be the first modern novel, as well as an incredibly important piece of Japanese literary history.

Why are the names important? Well... Hattori Hanzo is traditionally associated with the ninja clans of Iga, and in pop culture is often conceptualized as a ninja or associated with them. Genji, on the other hand, is a nobleman and warrior, very much embodying the traditional values and storytelling of Japanese nobility in the middle ages.

So there's an interesting, ironic inversion of their relationships there - Hanzo's name associated with the ninja, while Genji's name points towards samurai tradition.
---

So, here's me taking a bit of a risk. In this video we're going to be discussing a lot of real-world history and culture of Japan, and relating them back to the character pair of Hanzo and Genji and their relationship and interactions as a metaphor for the "soul" of Japan within the multicultural IP of Overwatch.

As I mention in the opening of the video, comments correcting my mistakes are EXTREMELY WELCOME. I've done my best to do my research, but the trouble with research is that the more research you do, the more aware you become of all the stuff you don't know about yet.

snippet.title: Riot Games are terrible at publishing comics - here's why, and ways to solve it
snippet.description:
UPDATE: Per Zoharan (see pinned comment), the Universe DOES have a filter feature to show comics under the "explore" subheading. They did not have that the last time I went looking around the site before making the video, but I'm VERY glad they've finally added it! It does seem to be missing the Kai'sa comic, the Camille release comic and the Spirit Guard Udyr comic, though.

-------------------

I have argued for a long time, and loudly, that comics are a fantastic way to explore the League of Legends IP. Riot Games, for their part, have been doing a much better job having comics made that do exactly that.

But, and I hate to put it so bluntly, they are terrible at publishing them. The most important thing when publishing, well, ANY content online, is discoverability: It needs to be as easy as possible for people to find the things you make. And on Riot's websites, discoverability is often almost nil.

Let's talk about that for a bit

snippet.title: WHAT CAN COMICS DO for League of Legends lore?
snippet.description:
MY OPINIONS IN SUMMARY:

- Comics are a fantastic way to do maintenance on overlooked and underexplored areas and characters in LoL without jeopardizing the canon or requiring massive resources to pull of successfully.

- Copy and exploit the advantages of models of publishing and franchise management used by Marvel, DC, Star Wars and other big media properties with huge numbers of characters.

- Outsource, bring in contractors, be ok with retconning and flexible canon, and most of all: INCREASE THE VOLUME OF OUTPUT

- Nothing is worse than silence. Lore needs to breathe to live, and not every breath needs to be a shout. Be OK with the low-impact, low-stakes story, be ok with treading water and letting the story simmer for a bit.

snippet.title: Same Face Syndrome - UPDATED!
snippet.description:
A while back I did a video on this subject. It really shouldn't have gotten popular or gotten any views. But it did. And I cringe at it.

SO WE'RE DOING IT AGAIN, AND DOING IT BETTER.

A lot of art - particularly manga and anime art - gets hit with "same face syndrome" as a criticism of its character design. But is it as good and relevant a criticism as we'd like?

TALKING POINTS:
- What is Same Face Syndrome?

- Why does it happen?
* Budget & time vs quality
* The Masking Effect

- What's the problem?
* Character design as storytelling

snippet.title: BLEACH and the danger of losing your theme
snippet.description:
REALITY PUNCH STUDIOS - Shonen Anime's Biggest Problem: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kLIbI1FI6N4
-----
Bleach might be one of my biggest disappointments as a manga, but it took me a long time to figure out exactly *why* its escalating power battles felt so much worse to me than they did in a story like Dragon Ball or One Piece.
Because Bleach is what happens when the ever-escalating need for more impressive power battles overtakes and obliterates the personal stakes of a story.
